{"slug": "static-vs-dynamic-websites-explained", "title": "Static vs Dynamic Websites, Explained Simply", "metaTitle": "Static vs Dynamic Websites, Explained Simply (2026)", "metaDescription": "What actually separates a static website from a dynamic one, real tradeoffs for speed, security, and personalization, and where AI-generated sites like Kodely fit today.", "targetKeyword": "static vs dynamic websites explained", "category": "Glossary", "bodyHtml": "

Every website you've ever visited falls into one of two categories: static or dynamic. The distinction sounds academic, but it actually determines how fast a site loads, how easy it is to secure, how much it costs to host, and whether it can show you something different from what it shows the next visitor. Here's what the terms actually mean, with no hand-waving.

Static websites: pre-built files, served as-is

A static website is a set of files — HTML, CSS, JavaScript, maybe some images — that were built ahead of time and sit on a server waiting to be handed to whoever asks for them. When you visit a static site, the server does not think. It does not query a database, run a template engine, or compute anything on your behalf. It just reads the files that already exist and sends them to your browser.

That means every visitor gets the same underlying files unless the site owner rebuilds and re-deploys them. A simple portfolio page — your name, a project list, a contact link — is a textbook static site. Whether it was hand-coded or produced by a static site generator, the output is the same: finished files, ready to serve.

Dynamic websites: built per request, usually from a database

A dynamic website generates its response at the moment you ask for it. The server runs code, often pulls data from a database, and assembles an HTML page tailored to that specific request before sending it back. A WordPress blog is dynamic in this sense — the server queries the database for post content on every visit. A logged-in dashboard is a sharper example: when you sign in, the server looks up your account, your data, your permissions, and builds a page that literally no one else would see. Refresh it tomorrow and it can be different again, because the underlying data changed.

The real tradeoffs

Neither approach is strictly better; they optimize for different things.

Static wins on speed, security, and hosting simplicity. Serving a pre-built file is about as fast as a server can go — there's no computation, no database round-trip, nothing to wait on. Security follows the same logic: there's no server-side application code processing your input, no database connection to compromise, no template engine to exploit. The attack surface shrinks to almost nothing because there's almost nothing running. Hosting is cheap and simple because you're just handing out files.

Dynamic wins on personalization and real-time data. If you need to show a user their own order history, a live inventory count, or content that changes based on who's logged in, you need a server that can compute that response per request. That capability costs something: you need server infrastructure, a database, application code to maintain, and a meaningfully larger surface for bugs and security issues to hide in.

The practical middle ground most real sites use is a static frontend that calls out to APIs from the browser for the personalized bits — you get the speed and simplicity of static hosting for the page itself, with dynamic data layered in via client-side requests after the page loads.

Static vs dynamic, side by side

FactorStaticDynamic
How content is producedPre-built once, served as-isGenerated per request on the server
Typical examplePortfolio site, marketing pageLogged-in dashboard, WordPress blog
Load speedVery fast — just file deliverySlower — depends on server/database work
Security surfaceSmall — no server logic to exploitLarger — server, database, auth all in play
Hosting complexitySimple, cheapNeeds a server and often a database
Per-user personalizationNot natively — needs client-side API callsNative — built into every request

Where Kodely's output fits, honestly

When you describe a site to Kodely in chat, it generates a real Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS app — actual component files, not a mockup. When you publish, that app gets compiled into a static bundle of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, and that compiled bundle is what actually gets served at your <name>.kodely.site address.

So the output Kodely publishes is static in the hosting sense described above: pre-built files served as-is, not regenerated per visitor by a server. That's exactly why it's fast and simple to host, and why every publish gets scanned for leaked secrets before going live — there's a small, well-defined set of files to check, not a live application with a database behind it.

Being static-served doesn't mean the site is inert, though. React adds real interactivity in the browser after the page loads — animations, state, interactive components all work fine. What it can't do yet is server-side personalization: showing a logged-in user their own data, because Kodely doesn't generate a backend, database, or authentication system today. That's the direct consequence of the architecture, not a missing checkbox — there's no server component to do that per-request computation on. Editing is chat-based (describe the change, Kodely updates the real components), every generation is a free checkpoint you can roll back to, and you can view and copy the generated source in-app, though there's no zip export yet.

If what you need is a fast, secure, easy-to-host site — portfolio, landing page, marketing site, small business presence — that's precisely the shape static output is good at. If you need per-user dashboards or server-side data, that's outside what Kodely builds right now.

Related terms

  • Static site generator (SSG): a tool that compiles source files into a static HTML/CSS/JS bundle ahead of time.
  • Server-side rendering (SSR): generating HTML on the server for each request, often to support dynamic or personalized content.
  • Client-side rendering (CSR): JavaScript in the browser builds or updates the page after the initial static files load — this is how a static-served React app gets its interactivity.
  • API call: a request a browser makes to fetch data after the page has loaded, the usual way static sites add dynamic-feeling data without a full backend.

FAQ

Is a static site the same as a "simple" or "unchangeable" site?

No. Static describes how a site is served — pre-built files handed out as-is — not whether it's basic or fixed forever. A static-served React app can have rich interactivity, animation, and client-side state; it just doesn't regenerate its HTML on the server for each visitor.

Can a static site show different content to different users at all?

Not from the server itself. But the page's JavaScript can call external APIs after loading to fetch and display personalized or live data in the browser — that's how many static sites layer in dynamic-feeling features without a server rendering each request.

Does Kodely generate a backend or database?

Not currently. Kodely generates and publishes a static-served React app — there's no backend, database, authentication, or payment generation yet, which is also why there's no server-side personalization in published sites.

Is Kodely's output fast because it's static?

Yes. Because a Kodely site is published as a pre-built bundle of files rather than regenerated per visit, there's no server-side computation standing between a visitor and the page loading.

Which one do I actually need?

If you're building a portfolio, landing page, or marketing site with no per-user data, static is simpler, faster, and cheaper to host and secure. If you need logged-in dashboards, user accounts, or real-time database-backed content, you need a dynamic backend — something outside what Kodely builds today.

Want to see what static-served, chat-built actually looks like? See it in action — build free. Or compare plans first on the pricing page.
